name: Chakma
catalog_citation: 藤原敬介 [Huziwara Keisuke]. 2019. チャクマ語音韻論 [Chakma phonology]. 『言語記述論集』 (Journal of Kijutsuken) 11: 51-102. Open at the RIHN repository, hdl http://id.nii.ac.jp/1422/00003020/ (https://chikyu.repo.nii.ac.jp/record/3103/files/gkr11_04_huziwara_51_102.pdf).
catalog_quote: チャクマ語には弁別的音調がある。音調のにない手は語の音節であり、各音節のピッチの高低が意味を区別する。すなわちチャクマ語における音調とは、当該音節における特定の音調の有無 (「高」か「低」かの「どちら」か) が問題となるアクセントであり、音調の種類 (「どの」か) が問題となるトーンではない [...] 本稿ではこのアクセントを音素とみなし、ピッチが高いところを/ ´ /でしめす。音調としてはピッチとは別にストレスもあるが、これは弁別的ではないとかんがえるので音素とはみとめない。[pp. 54-55] [...] 筆者の観察によれば、チャクマ語のアクセントには意味の相違に関与するピッチと、意味の相違には関与しないストレスとがある。[p. 69] ピッチは歴史的に有気音のあった直後の母音で高くなる傾向にある。[...] ストレスは一音節語ではピッチの高い音節にある。二音節以上の語では、アクセントをもたない語では第一音節にあり、アクセントをもつ語ではアクセントをになう音節にあるのが一般的である [p. 70] [n.45:] チャクマ語ではアクセントが高いところから低いところになる変わり目でストレスがあるようにきこえる傾向がある。[...] [sec. 3.1:] ストレスは音韻論的には無視してよいので表記しない。[p. 70] [(78):] a. át (●) 「手」 b. at (○)「八」

new_statements.translation: Chakma has distinctive pitch. The bearer of pitch is the syllable of the word, and the high vs. low pitch of each syllable distinguishes meaning. [...] In this paper I treat this accent as phonemic and mark the high-pitched place with an acute. Besides pitch there is also stress, but since I consider it non-distinctive I do not recognize it as phonemic. [...] According to my observations, Chakma accent comprises pitch, which is involved in meaning differences, and stress, which is not. [...] In monosyllabic words stress is on the high-pitched syllable. In words of two or more syllables, it is generally on the first syllable in words that have no accent, and on the accent-bearing syllable in words that have an accent.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Chakma (Khagrachhari dialect) is described as a pitch accent language: every syllable is lexically H (accented) or L, with minimal pairs (át 'hand' / at 'eight', gác 'grass' / gac 'tree'); H historically arose on vowels following aspirates, h or sibilants and is then redistributed by an assimilation/dissimilation rule (*V[α accent] > V[-α accent] after an accented V). Stress is present but non-contrastive and predictable from the pitch pattern: it falls on the (first) H syllable of an accented word and on the initial syllable of an all-L word; the author does not transcribe it.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No secondary stress described. For disyllables (p.71, (87)): HH words have stress on the first syllable only; HL first syllable stressed; LH second syllable 'slightly' stressed; LL first syllable may sound slightly stressed because its pitch is a little higher (n.45).
new_statements.exceptions: Accent (pitch) placement exceptions: some noun plurals, trisyllabic verb infinitives (dagana LLL vs cúnáná HHH vs pÉlána HHL vs dEganá LLH), and compound nouns are not predicted by the accent rules (secs. 4.2, 5.2, 6). One loan (sec. 2.4.7 n.) has unexplained accent. No exceptions stated for the stress generalization beyond 'generally' (一般的である).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (stem plus affixes = domain of the accent rules, sec. 3.1); data are elicited citation forms from a single consultant (Mithun Chakma, Khagrachhari, Chittagong Hill Tracts) collected 1999-2001 for the author's 2001 Kyoto University MA thesis, published essentially unchanged in 2019. Contrasts with Ganguly & Talukdar 1996: 1651, who assert no tone and 'equal stress' on all syllables; Yagi 1964b and Maniruzzaman 1984 (quoted by Huziwara) both also report a pitch/tone contrast.
new_statements.identity_note: Huziwara 2019 explicitly describes the Khagrachhari (カグラチョリ) dialect of Chakma, Chittagong Hill Tracts, Bangladesh, from one Dhaka-University-student consultant; Glottolog chak1266 has no dialect subcodes. Bhattacharyya 2004 describes Kolkata (diaspora) Chakma and Rangamati Chakma; Ganguly & Talukdar 1996 describe Indian (Tripura/Mizoram) Chakma generically. The closely related Tangchangya (tang1330) is treated by some as a Chakma dialect but is not covered by any of these.

sources.note: Khagrachhari Chakma has a distinctive (privative) pitch accent: each syllable is H (accented) or L, minimal pairs át 'hand' vs at 'eight' etc. (sec. 2.1.3 p.54-55, sec. 3 p.69-72). Stress exists but is non-distinctive and not transcribed: in monosyllables on the H syllable; in polysyllables on the first syllable of accentless words and on the accent-bearing syllable of accented words (p.70, n.45: heard at the H-to-L transition). Secs. 4-5 derive accent placement: H arose after historical aspirates/h/sibilants, then *V[α acc] > V[-α acc] / V́__ (assimilation/dissimilation); exceptions in noun…

sources.note: p.1651 (image-only PDF, scanned): 'Chakma is not a tonal language. That is to say the change of tone does not change the meanings of words. Besides intonation patterns like those of English where some words and syllables are stressed more than the others is not observable in Chakma. All the syllables in a word and all the words in a sentence get equal stress like most of the Indo-Aryan languages.' Impressionistic sketch; contradicted by Huziwara 2019 (who finds contrastive pitch) and criticized by him (n.7) as unreliable.

sources.note: Chapter 2 Phonology (pp. 9-101; Kolkata Chakma and Rangamati Chakma) is purely segmental (vowels, consonants, gemination, clusters, syllable structure); a full-text search for stress/accent ch.1, ch.2, ch.5 and the conclusion finds no mention of stress, accent, tone or pitch. Silent on stress.
